name: str_split_fixed
title: Split up a string into pieces

origin.description: Split each string into a fixed number of pieces and return a character matrix.

arguments.name: string
arguments.text: Input vector. Either a character vector, or something coercible to one.

arguments.name: pattern
arguments.text: Pattern to look for. The default interpretation is a regular expression. regex() sets the flags. fixed() compares literal text. coll() uses Unicode collation for a locale. boundary() matches character, word, line, and sentence boundaries. The empty string "" is equivalent to boundary("character").

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Number of columns. If an input has fewer pieces, the row is padded with "". Inf is allowed and then the width is the longest split, because the unlimited count does not force extra columns.

origin.details: string and pattern are checked with vctrs::vec_size_common, then n is checked, then the call is str_split(string, pattern, n = n, simplify = TRUE). Short rows are padded with empty strings, not with NA. The empty pattern is still a character boundary, so str_split_fixed("", "", 2) is two empty strings: the empty input has no pieces, and the matrix pads them.
origin.value: A character matrix with n columns and one row per string. In the check it is stored as a list of rows.
origin.example:
fruits <- c(
  "apples and oranges and pears and bananas",
  "pineapples and mangos and guavas"
)
str_split_fixed(fruits, " and ", 3)
str_split_fixed(fruits, " and ", 4)

translation.description: Split each string into n columns, padding short rows with empty strings.

arguments.name: string
arguments.text: A string, stringi._na.NA, or a list of those. None is an empty character vector.

arguments.name: pattern
arguments.text: Passed to str_split. A plain string is a regular expression. "" is a character boundary.

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Column count. A whole number of at least 1, or float("inf"). 0 is an error. The pad is "", not NA.

translation.details: check_lengths runs here and again inside str_split. The call is str_split(..., simplify=True). Each inner list is one row. A short row is extended with "". float("inf") is the unlimited split, so the width is the longest row rather than an infinite pad.
translation.value: A list of rows. Each row is a list of n strings, padded with "" when the split is shorter.
translation.example:
from stringr.split import str_split_fixed

fruits = [
    "apples and oranges and pears and bananas",
    "pineapples and mangos and guavas",
]
print(str_split_fixed(fruits, " and ", 3))
print(str_split_fixed(fruits, " and ", 4))
